line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bb4 Nxc6
teaches: When a pin threatens to win your central pawn, do not look for a way to hold the pawn — look for the piece whose capture the pin is aiming at, and trade the piece that supports the threat. Removing one attacker from the equation is worth more than adding a defender, because it also gains time if the trade comes with hits of its own.
explains: Taking on c6 hits the bishop on b4 and the queen behind it while it removes the knight, so the capture cannot simply be ignored. With that knight gone the central pawn can be reinforced next move without the pin costing anything.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bb4 Nxc6 Bxc3+ bxc3 bxc6 Bd3
teaches: A bishop blocked by its own pawn is not automatically misplaced. If the pawn it stares at is the one holding your space, the bishop is doing the most valuable job on the board — bad bishops defend good pawns — and the moment that pawn advances, the same bishop becomes the best piece you own. Judge a piece by the job, not by the diagonal.
explains: The bishop comes to d3 holding the pawn on e4 and the pawn on c2 behind it. It has no open diagonal today, and it is the reason the centre stands.
